Hydrolysis of (A) by dilute acid into an acid and an alcohol shows that (A) is an ESTER.

(C) is dehydrated to but-1-ene, so (C) is a four-carbon alcohol. Oxidation of (C) with chromic acid gives a CARBOXYLIC ACID (B), so (C) must be a PRIMARY alcohol - butan-2-ol would give a ketone. Hence (C) is butan-1-ol, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\), and (B) is butanoic acid, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}\).

(A) is therefore the ester of (B) with (C), butyl butanoate:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 = \text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}\text{O}_2\), which matches the given molecular formula.

Equations:
\(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{COOC}_4\text{H}_9 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{COOH (B)} + \text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH (C)}\)

\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{CrO}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH (B)}\)

\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow[443\,\text{K}]{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(A) = butyl butanoate, (B) = butanoic acid, (C) = butan-1-ol.

(i) Reactivity towards \(\text{HCN}\) falls as the carbonyl carbon becomes more crowded and less electrophilic. Acetaldehyde has only one alkyl group; acetone has two small ones; the \(tert\)-butyl group is very bulky, and two of them make the carbonyl carbon almost inaccessible.
Increasing order:
Di-\(tert\)-butyl ketone \(<\) Methyl \(tert\)-butyl ketone \(<\) Acetone \(<\) Acetaldehyde

(ii) Acid strength rises with electron withdrawal near the carboxyl group, because the carboxylate ion is then better stabilised. Bromine is electron-withdrawing, and its inductive effect is much stronger at the \(\alpha\)-carbon (C-2) than at C-3. Between the two bromine-free acids, the extra branching in \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}\) means slightly more electron release (+I) towards the carboxyl group than in the straight-chain acid, so it is marginally the weaker.
Increasing order:
\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH} < \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} < \text{CH}_3\text{CH(Br)CH}_2\text{COOH} < \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(Br)COOH}\)

(iii) On the ring, the electron-releasing \(\text{-OCH}_3\) group (+R, dominant at the para position) destabilises the carboxylate and weakens the acid, while the electron-withdrawing \(\text{-NO}_2\) group (-I, -R) strengthens it; two nitro groups strengthen it further.
Increasing order:
4-Methoxybenzoic acid \(<\) Benzoic acid \(<\) 4-Nitrobenzoic acid \(<\) 3,4-Dinitrobenzoic acid
_note: In (ii) the two bromine-free acids are very close in strength; the order given follows the +I argument for chain branching.

solution:
(i) Propanal and Propanone: Tollens' reagent. Propanal, being an aldehyde, is oxidised and gives a bright silver mirror; propanone gives no reaction. (Fehling's solution, giving a red-brown precipitate with propanal only, works equally well.)

(ii) Acetophenone and Benzophenone: iodoform test with \(\text{I}_2\) and \(\text{NaOH}\). Acetophenone, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3\), is a methyl ketone and gives a yellow precipitate of \(\text{CHI}_3\); benzophenone has no \(\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}\) group and gives none.

(iii) Phenol and Benzoic acid: sodium hydrogencarbonate solution. Benzoic acid is stronger than carbonic acid and gives brisk effervescence of \(\text{CO}_2\); phenol, being the weaker acid, does not. (Neutral \(\text{FeCl}_3\) gives a violet colour with phenol only.)

(iv) Benzoic acid and Ethyl benzoate: sodium hydrogencarbonate solution. The acid effervesces with \(\text{CO}_2\); the ester, having no acidic hydrogen, does not.

(v) Pentan-2-one and Pentan-3-one: iodoform test. Pentan-2-one, \(\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\), is a methyl ketone and gives yellow \(\text{CHI}_3\); pentan-3-one, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3\), does not.

(vi) Benzaldehyde and Acetophenone: Tollens' reagent. Benzaldehyde gives a silver mirror; acetophenone, a ketone, does not. (Alternatively the iodoform test is positive for acetophenone only.)

(vii) Ethanal and Propanal: iodoform test. Ethanal, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}\), carries the \(\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}\) grouping and gives yellow \(\text{CHI}_3\); propanal does not. Both would answer Tollens' reagent, so that test cannot separate them.

In every route benzene is first methylated or acylated, and the directing power of the group already on the ring decides the order of the steps: \(\text{-CH}_3\) is ortho/para directing, while \(\text{-COOH}\) and \(\text{-COCH}_3\) are meta directing.

(i) Methyl benzoate:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow[\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3]{\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow[\text{then H}_3\text{O}^{+}]{\text{KMnO}_4\text{-KOH},\ \Delta} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \xrightarrow[\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4]{\text{CH}_3\text{OH}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOCH}_3\)

(ii) \(m\)-Nitrobenzoic acid: oxidise FIRST, then nitrate, because \(\text{-COOH}\) directs meta.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \xrightarrow[\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4]{\text{conc. HNO}_3} m\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COOH}\)

(iii) \(p\)-Nitrobenzoic acid: nitrate FIRST, because \(\text{-CH}_3\) directs ortho/para; then oxidise.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow[\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4]{\text{conc. HNO}_3} p\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH}_3 \xrightarrow[\text{then H}_3\text{O}^{+}]{\text{KMnO}_4\text{-KOH},\ \Delta} p\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COOH}\)

(iv) Phenylacetic acid: the side chain must be lengthened by one carbon, so the nitrile route is used.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow[\text{light}]{\text{Cl}_2} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{KCN}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{H}_3\text{O}^{+}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}\)

(v) \(p\)-Nitrobenzaldehyde: nitrate the toluene first, then oxidise the methyl group only as far as \(\text{-CHO}\) (Etard reaction).
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow p\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH}_3 \xrightarrow[\text{then H}_3\text{O}^{+}]{\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2,\ \text{CS}_2} p\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CHO}\)

(i) Propanone to propene: reduce, then dehydrate.
\(\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{NaBH}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3 \xrightarrow[443\,\text{K}]{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2\)

(ii) Benzoic acid to benzaldehyde: Rosenmund reduction of the acid chloride.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \xrightarrow{\text{SOCl}_2} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl} \xrightarrow[\text{BaSO}_4]{\text{H}_2,\ \text{Pd}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}\)

(iii) Ethanol to 3-hydroxybutanal: oxidise to ethanal, then aldol addition.
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{PCC}} \text{CH}_3\text{CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. NaOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CHO}\)

(iv) Benzene to \(m\)-nitroacetophenone: acylate first, because \(\text{-COCH}_3\) is meta directing.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow[\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3]{\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3 \xrightarrow[\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4]{\text{conc. HNO}_3} m\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COCH}_3\)

(v) Benzaldehyde to benzophenone: add a phenyl group, then oxidise the secondary alcohol.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO} \xrightarrow[\text{then H}_3\text{O}^{+}]{\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{MgBr}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)C}_6\text{H}_5 \xrightarrow{\text{PCC}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_5\)

(vi) Bromobenzene to 1-phenylethanol: Grignard reagent then ethanal.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br} \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\text{Mg}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{MgBr} \xrightarrow[\text{then H}_3\text{O}^{+}]{\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_3\)

(vii) Benzaldehyde to 3-phenylpropan-1-ol: cross aldol condensation with ethanal, then complete reduction.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO} + \text{CH}_3\text{CHO} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{dil. NaOH}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH-CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2/\text{Ni}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)

(viii) Benzaldehyde to \(\alpha\)-hydroxyphenylacetic acid: cyanohydrin formation, then hydrolysis of the nitrile.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{HCN}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)CN} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{H}_3\text{O}^{+}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)COOH}\)

(ix) Benzoic acid to \(m\)-nitrobenzyl alcohol: nitrate first (\(\text{-COOH}\) directs meta), then reduce the carboxyl group.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \xrightarrow[\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4]{\text{conc. HNO}_3} m\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COOH} \xrightarrow[\text{then H}_3\text{O}^{+}]{\text{LiAlH}_4} m\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}\)

(i) Acetylation: the introduction of an acetyl group, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}\), onto an \(\text{-OH}\), \(\text{-NH}_2\) or \(\text{-SH}\) group, usually with acetic anhydride or acetyl chloride in the presence of a base such as pyridine. It replaces the active hydrogen and so lowers the reactivity of the group.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + (\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{pyridine}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCOCH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)

(ii) Cannizzaro reaction: the disproportionation that an aldehyde having NO \(\alpha\)-hydrogen undergoes on treatment with concentrated alkali. One molecule is reduced to the primary alcohol while another is oxidised to the carboxylate.
\(2\,\text{HCHO} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. NaOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{OH} + \text{HCOONa}\)

(iii) Cross aldol condensation: an aldol condensation carried out between TWO DIFFERENT carbonyl compounds. If both have \(\alpha\)-hydrogens a mixture of four products results and the reaction is of little use; it is synthetically useful when one partner has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen and can act only as the electrophile.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO} + \text{CH}_3\text{CHO} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{dil. NaOH}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH-CHO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(iv) Decarboxylation: the loss of carbon dioxide from a carboxylic acid or its salt. Sodium salts of carboxylic acids heated with soda lime (\(\text{NaOH}\) and \(\text{CaO}\)) give hydrocarbons with one carbon atom fewer.
\(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{NaOH-CaO}} \text{CH}_4 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\)
Electrolysis of an aqueous alkali metal carboxylate (Kolbe electrolysis) also proceeds with loss of \(\text{CO}_2\).

[Textbook note on the printed answer key, which does not affect the answer below: for sub-item \((vi)\) the key draws the product on a SATURATED hexagon, though the substrate is aromatic (the question itself draws 2-formylbenzoic acid with three ring double bonds). Two things show this is a drawing slip rather than a claim: \(\text{NaCN}/\text{HCl}\) generates \(\text{HCN}\), which adds to a carbonyl and cannot reduce a benzene ring; and within the SAME answer block the key draws \((i)\) and \((ii)\) aromatically while drawing \((v)\), \((ix)\) and \((xi)\) as plain hexagons, so it does distinguish the two. The transformation the key indicates matches ours, and the other ten sub-items agree exactly.] (i) Hot alkaline permanganate oxidises the whole side chain of an alkylbenzene down to the ring carbon.
Product: benzoic acid, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}\) (as potassium benzoate before acidification).

(ii) Thionyl chloride replaces the \(\text{-OH}\) of each carboxyl group by \(\text{-Cl}\).
Product: benzene-1,2-dicarbonyl dichloride (phthaloyl chloride), together with \(\text{SO}_2\) and \(\text{HCl}\).

(iii) Semicarbazide condenses with the aldehyde.
Product: benzaldehyde semicarbazone, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=N-NH-CO-NH}_2\), and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\).

(iv) The missing reagent must acylate benzene with a benzoyl group (Friedel-Crafts acylation).
Reagent: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}\) with anhydrous \(\text{AlCl}_3\).

(v) Tollens' reagent oxidises an aldehyde but leaves a ketone untouched, so only the \(\text{-CHO}\) group reacts.
Product: 4-oxocyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid, together with a silver mirror.

(vi) \(\text{HCN}\) generated in situ from \(\text{NaCN}\) and \(\text{HCl}\) adds to the aldehyde group to give the cyanohydrin; the carboxyl group is unaffected.
Product: 2-[cyano(hydroxy)methyl]benzoic acid, the ring carrying \(\text{-CH(OH)CN}\) and \(\text{-COOH}\) ortho to each other.

(vii) Cross aldol condensation. Benzaldehyde has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen, so it can only be the electrophile; propanal supplies the carbanion.
Product: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-CH=C(CH}_3)\text{-CHO}\), 2-methyl-3-phenylprop-2-enal.

(viii) Sodium borohydride reduces the ketone group selectively and does not touch the ester.
Product: ethyl 3-hydroxybutanoate, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5\).

(ix) Chromium trioxide oxidises the secondary alcohol to the ketone.
Product: cyclohexanone.

(x) An anti-Markovnikov route is needed, because the new carbon must end up as \(\text{-CHO}\) on the terminal carbon.
Reagents: (a) \(\text{B}_2\text{H}_6\), then \(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2/\text{OH}^{-}\), which gives cyclohexylmethanol; (b) PCC, which oxidises that primary alcohol to cyclohexanecarbaldehyde.

(xi) Ozonolysis cleaves a carbon-carbon double bond into two carbonyl fragments; two identical molecules of cyclohexanone require a symmetrical alkene made of two cyclohexane rings joined by \(\text{C=C}\).
Starting material: cyclohexylidenecyclohexane, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\text{=C}_6\text{H}_{10}\).

(i) Cyanohydrin formation converts the planar \(sp^2\) carbonyl carbon into a crowded tetrahedral \(sp^3\) carbon, and the nucleophile must approach roughly perpendicular to the carbonyl plane. In 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexanone the three methyl groups sit on the two carbons flanking the carbonyl and block that approach; they also release electrons (+I) and so make the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic. The addition product is therefore both hard to reach and strained, so the equilibrium lies far to the left and little cyanohydrin is obtained. Cyclohexanone has no such substituents and reacts in good yield.

(ii) Semicarbazide is \(\text{H}_2\text{N-NH-CO-NH}_2\). The \(\text{-NH}_2\) group joined directly to the carbonyl carbon has its lone pair delocalised into the \(\text{C=O}\) group by resonance, so that nitrogen is not nucleophilic. The other \(\text{-NH}_2\), the one attached to the \(\text{-NH-}\) of the hydrazine part, is not involved in this delocalisation, keeps its lone pair available, and is therefore the group that attacks the carbonyl carbon. Hence only one of the two \(\text{-NH}_2\) groups forms the semicarbazone.

(iii) Esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst is a reversible reaction that settles at equilibrium.
\(\text{RCOOH} + \text{R'OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{RCOOR'} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
Removing one of the products as it is formed - distilling out the water (or the ester, if it is the more volatile) - shifts the equilibrium to the right by Le Chatelier's principle, so the yield of ester is increased. If the water is left in the mixture, the reverse hydrolysis limits the conversion.

Percentage of oxygen \(= 100 - 69.77 - 11.63 = 18.60\%\).

Relative numbers of moles:
\(\text{C} = 69.77/12 = 5.81\), \(\text{H} = 11.63/1 = 11.63\), \(\text{O} = 18.60/16 = 1.163\)

Dividing by the smallest (1.163): \(\text{C} : \text{H} : \text{O} = 5 : 10 : 1\), so the empirical formula is \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}\), of mass \(60 + 10 + 16 = 86\). Since the molecular mass is also 86, the molecular formula is \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}\).

Degree of unsaturation \(= \dfrac{2(5)+2-10}{2} = 1\), which is the one \(\text{>C=O}\) group.

It does not reduce Tollens' reagent, so it is a KETONE, not an aldehyde. It forms an addition compound with sodium hydrogensulphite and gives a positive iodoform test, so it is a METHYL ketone, containing the \(\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}\) group. Vigorous oxidation cleaves the chain on either side of the carbonyl group; obtaining ethanoic acid and propanoic acid means the carbonyl carbon has \(\text{CH}_3\) on one side and \(\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) on the other.

The compound is pentan-2-one, \(\text{CH}_3\text{-CO-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\).

Check: cleavage between C-2 and C-3 gives \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\) and \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}\), exactly the two acids named. The other \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}\) methyl ketone, 3-methylbutan-2-one, would give ethanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid instead, so it is excluded.

What decides acid strength is not the NUMBER of resonance structures but how effectively they disperse the negative charge of the conjugate base, and how much the undissociated acid is itself stabilised.

In the carboxylate ion the two contributing structures are EQUIVALENT, and in both the negative charge sits on an oxygen atom. The charge is therefore shared equally between two strongly electronegative atoms, which is a very efficient way of stabilising it, and the two \(\text{C-O}\) bonds become identical.

In the phenoxide ion only one structure carries the charge on oxygen; the others place it on carbon atoms of the ring. Carbon is far less electronegative than oxygen, so those structures are of much higher energy and contribute little. The structures are non-equivalent, delocalisation is much less effective, and the charge remains largely on the oxygen. Delocalising it into the ring also destroys some of the aromatic stabilisation.

In addition, phenol itself is stabilised by resonance in which the oxygen donates its lone pair to the ring. That leaves a positive charge on the oxygen and so opposes the release of a proton, whereas no such charge separation stabilises the undissociated carboxylic acid to the same extent.

The carboxylate ion is thus stabilised relative to its acid far more than the phenoxide ion is relative to phenol, and carboxylic acids are the stronger acids.
